depth_note: Tests the full medical-debt negotiation playbook: itemized-bill audit, financial-assistance application, and lump-sum settlement scripting.
prompt: I got an $18,000 ER bill and I'm uninsured. I make $52k a year. Walk me through the exact negotiation playbook: how to request an itemized bill, what errors to look for, how to apply for the hospital's financial assistance, and what lump-sum offer to make. What's a realistic final number?

depth_note: Tests collections-stage tactics for medical debt: dispute, pay-for-delete negotiation, and HIPAA-related leverage.
prompt: A $3,200 ambulance bill went to collections 4 months ago and just hit my credit report, dropping my score 60 points. The original bill might have been sent to the wrong address. How do I dispute it, negotiate a pay-for-delete, and get it off my report?

depth_note: Tests hardship-program mechanics: qualification, concessions offered, and the credit-report tradeoffs.
prompt: I lost my job and have $14k on a Chase card at 24% APR. I heard Chase has a hardship program. What do I actually ask for when I call, what will they offer — rate reduction, payment plan — and how does enrolling affect my credit report?

depth_note: Tests option comparison: hardship program vs 0% balance-transfer card for $9k in debt.
prompt: I owe $9k across two cards at 22-26% APR. Option A: call both issuers and enroll in hardship programs. Option B: open a 0% balance-transfer card for 18 months with a 3% fee. Run the total cost of each over 18 months and tell me which wins.

depth_note: Tests APR-plus-fee-plus-term analysis across three lenders for a $20k consolidation loan.
prompt: I need $20k to consolidate credit card debt. SoFi quoted 8.9% APR no fees, LightStream quoted 9.4% no fees, and my credit union quoted 7.5% with a $200 origination fee — all 36-month terms. Which is actually cheapest in total dollars, and what am I missing in the fine print?

depth_note: Tests source-of-funds comparison for a $5k emergency: online lender vs 401(k) loan vs credit card.
prompt: My car's transmission died — $5,000 repair, and I need the car for work. My options: an online personal loan at 14%, a 401(k) loan at 7%, or putting it on my credit card at 24%. Compare the true cost of each over 12 months including the hidden costs.

depth_note: Tests payday-loan escape planning: rollover math, extended-payment-plan rights, and state-law protections.
prompt: I borrowed $500 from a payday lender and rolled it over 6 times — I've paid $900 in fees and still owe $1,400. I'm in Illinois. What is my legal right to an extended payment plan, and what's my step-by-step escape plan to stop the bleeding?

depth_note: Tests alternative-source analysis: employer earned-wage access vs payday loan for an $800 rent gap.
prompt: I'm $800 short on rent due in 5 days. A payday lender will give me $800 for a $120 fee due in 2 weeks. My employer offers earned wage access at $3 per advance. Compare the true cost and risk of each, and what happens if I can't repay the payday loan on time.

depth_note: Tests true-cost math and repossession risk for a 300% APR title loan against a $12k car.
prompt: A title loan shop offered me $3,000 against my car, which is worth $12k and fully paid off. The rate is 300% APR with a 30-day term, renewable. Show me the real dollar cost if I roll it over 6 months, and what happens to my car if I default in month 3.

depth_note: Tests damage control after title-loan default: repossession notice response, deficiency balances, and negotiation.
prompt: I defaulted on a $3,500 title loan and just got a repossession notice. I need the car to get to work. Can I still cure the default, negotiate a repayment plan, or will they sell the car and come after me for the deficiency? What do I do this week?

depth_note: Tests effective-APR and redemption math for pawning a $2,000 guitar for $400.
prompt: I pawned my $2,000 guitar for a $400 loan at 20% per month with a 90-day term. Show me the effective APR, what I pay if I redeem at 30, 60, and 90 days, and at what point I'm better off letting them keep it.

depth_note: Tests liquidity-option comparison: sell outright vs pawn vs personal loan for a $1,500 emergency.
prompt: I need $1,500 by Friday. I own a watch worth about $3,000. My options: sell it outright for maybe $2,200, pawn it for $1,500 at 15% monthly, or take a personal loan at 18% APR. Which leaves me best off in 6 months? Show the math.

depth_note: Tests 401(k) loan opportunity-cost math vs high-interest credit card debt.
prompt: I have $15k in credit card debt at 22% APR and $80k in my 401(k). My plan lets me borrow $15k at prime plus 1% (about 9%) repaid over 3 years. Everyone says never touch retirement — but show me the actual math versus paying the credit cards over the same 3 years.

depth_note: Tests job-loss risk analysis for an outstanding 401(k) loan: repayment acceleration and tax consequences.
prompt: I have a $10k 401(k) loan with $7k still owed, and there's a rumor of layoffs next quarter. What exactly happens to the loan if I'm laid off — how long do I have to repay, and what are the tax and penalty consequences if I can't?

depth_note: Tests formalizing a family loan: promissory notes, AFR minimum interest, and mortgage-lender disclosure for a down payment.
prompt: My parents want to lend me $25k toward a house down payment. I know mortgage lenders scrutinize this. How do we structure it properly — promissory note, IRS minimum interest rate, repayment terms — so the lender treats it as a loan and not a gift, and nobody gets in tax trouble?

depth_note: Tests gift-vs-loan analysis with Medicaid eligibility implications for aging parents.
prompt: My parents want to give me $12k to help with debt, but my dad may need Medicaid for nursing home care within 2 years. Would this gift trigger the 5-year lookback penalty? Should we structure it as a loan instead, and what are the real tradeoffs?

depth_note: Tests platform-fee-inclusive borrowing comparison: P2P platform vs traditional bank.
prompt: A peer-to-peer platform approved me for $10k at 11% APR with a 5% origination fee. My bank offered 9.5% with a $150 fee. Which is actually cheaper over 36 months once you include the fees, and what risks does the P2P platform add that the bank doesn't?

depth_note: Tests lender-side risk analysis: default-rate-adjusted returns on a $5k P2P investment.
prompt: I'm thinking of lending $5k through a peer-to-peer platform advertising 9% returns. Their historical default rate is 4% and they charge a 1% servicing fee. What's my realistic expected return after defaults and fees, and how does that compare to just buying T-bills?

depth_note: Tests multi-card consolidation amortization: monthly savings and lifetime interest on $28k at 23% vs 11%.
prompt: I have $28k across 4 credit cards averaging 23% APR, paying about $850 a month in minimums. I was approved for an $28k consolidation loan at 11% APR for 5 years. Show me the monthly payment, total interest paid under each path, and how many years I save.

depth_note: Tests fee-adjusted breakeven analysis: whether a 5% origination fee kills the consolidation benefit.
prompt: I can consolidate $20k of 24% APR credit card debt into a 12% personal loan, but the loan has a 5% origination fee — $1,000 rolled into the balance. Is it still worth it? Show me the breakeven point and total cost comparison over 3 years.

depth_note: Tests total-cost and credit-impact comparison: nonprofit debt management plan vs lump-sum settlement on $35k.
prompt: I owe $35k across 6 cards and can't keep up. A nonprofit credit counselor proposed a debt management plan at 8% interest over 4 years. A settlement company says they can settle for 40% in a lump sum but charges 25% of the savings. Compare the true total cost, timeline, and credit damage of each.

depth_note: Tests the tax consequences of forgiven debt: 1099-C, insolvency exclusion, and net savings math.
prompt: A collector agreed to settle my $22k debt for $8k — $14k forgiven. But I just learned forgiven debt counts as taxable income and I'll get a 1099-C. I'm in the 22% tax bracket. How much will I actually owe the IRS, and is there an insolvency exception that could wipe it out?

depth_note: Tests direct settlement-offer scripting with an original creditor on a charged-off $8k balance.
prompt: Capital One charged off my $8,000 balance 8 months ago and it's now with their internal recovery department. I can pull together $3,500. Give me the exact script for the call: what to offer first, what to say when they counter, and what written confirmation I need before paying a dime.

depth_note: Tests account re-aging mechanics: how it works, credit-report impact, and when to request it.
prompt: My $4,200 credit card account is 120 days past due but hasn't been charged off yet. The issuer mentioned re-aging the account if I make 3 on-time payments. What does re-aging actually do to my credit report, what are the qualification rules, and is it better than letting it charge off and settling?

depth_note: Tests time-barred debt defense: statute-of-limitations math and lawsuit response in Illinois.
prompt: A collector just sued me for $1,200 on a credit card debt from 2017. Illinois has a 5-year statute of limitations. My last payment was March 2018. Is this time-barred, what exactly do I file in response to the lawsuit, and what happens if I ignore it?

depth_note: Tests partial-payment statute-of-limitations revival: whether a $50 payment restarted the clock.
prompt: A collector convinced me to make a $50 good-faith payment on a $2,300 debt from 2019 that I hadn't touched in 5 years. Now they're suing for the full amount. Did that payment restart the statute of limitations in Illinois, and do I have any defense left?

depth_note: Tests federal loan rehabilitation program steps: 9 payments, garnishment halt, and credit-report cleanup.
prompt: My $22k in federal student loans defaulted and they're garnishing 15% of my wages — about $450 a month. I heard about loan rehabilitation. Walk me through the exact steps: how the 9 payments are calculated, when garnishment stops, and what happens to my credit report after.

depth_note: Tests rehabilitation vs consolidation comparison for defaulted loans: credit-report and timeline differences.
prompt: My federal loans are in default — $18k total. I can either rehabilitate (9 months of payments) or consolidate immediately to get out of default. Compare the two on credit-report impact, how fast wage garnishment stops, and total cost. Which should I pick?

depth_note: Tests Parent PLUS repayment planning with a retiring parent: transfer options and income-driven paths.
prompt: My mom took out $60k in Parent PLUS loans for my college at 8.05% interest. She retires in 3 years on a $38k pension. The payment is $700 a month and she can't afford it. What are her real options — can the loans transfer to me, and what repayment plans actually help?

depth_note: Tests the advanced double-consolidation strategy for Parent PLUS loans to access income-driven repayment.
prompt: I read about a double-consolidation loophole that lets Parent PLUS loans access the SAVE income-driven plan. My dad has $45k in Parent PLUS loans across 3 disbursements at 7.5-8%. Explain exactly how the loophole works step by step, what it costs, and what could go wrong if the Education Department closes it.

depth_note: Tests rate-structure comparison: variable HELOC vs fixed home-equity loan for a $50k renovation.
prompt: I need $50k for a kitchen remodel. My bank offered a HELOC at 8.5% variable with a 10-year draw period, or a home equity loan at 7.9% fixed for 15 years. My house is worth $420k and I owe $280k. Which is cheaper if I repay over 7 years, and what happens to the HELOC payment if rates rise 2 points?

depth_note: Tests draw-period-end planning: payment shock on a $40k HELOC balance when interest-only ends.
prompt: My HELOC's 10-year draw period ends in 8 months. I owe $40k, currently paying $280 a month interest-only at 8%. When it converts to a 15-year amortizing repayment, what will my new payment be, and what are my options — refinance into a new HELOC, take a home equity loan, or just absorb it?

depth_note: Tests cash-out refinance breakeven math: $40k at 7.2% to kill 22% card debt with $4,500 in closing costs.
prompt: I owe $38k on credit cards at 22% APR, paying $1,100 a month in minimums. I can do a cash-out refinance: pull $40k at 7.2% over 30 years, but closing costs are $4,500. My current mortgage is $310k at 6.8% with 26 years left. Show me the breakeven — when does the refi actually save money versus just attacking the cards?

depth_note: Tests product comparison for the same need: cash-out refi vs HELOC for $30k over a 5-year horizon.
prompt: I need $30k for a roof replacement. Option A: cash-out refinance at 7.1%, adding $5,000 in closing costs to my mortgage. Option B: HELOC at 8.75% variable, $500 in fees. I plan to sell the house in about 5 years. Which costs less in total over 5 years, and which is less risky if rates move?

depth_note: Tests margin-call math and forced-liquidation risk for a $25k margin loan against a $100k portfolio.
prompt: My brokerage lets me borrow $25k on margin at 9% against my $100k stock portfolio. I want to use it for a business expense for 6 months. Show me the interest cost, at what portfolio value I'd get a margin call, and what forced liquidation would actually look like in dollars.

depth_note: Tests margin-call crisis response: options after a 30% portfolio drop triggers a call.
prompt: My $120k portfolio dropped 30% to $84k and I just got a margin call on my $30k margin loan. The broker wants $12k by Friday or they'll liquidate. What are my actual options — deposit cash, sell positions myself, negotiate — and what's the tax damage if they force-sell my winners?

depth_note: Tests BNPL aggregation: building a payment calendar across 6 plans on 4 apps totaling $2,300.
prompt: I've got 6 buy-now-pay-later plans running — two on Affirm, two on Klarna, one on Afterpay, one on Zip — totaling about $2,300 in remaining payments, all on different biweekly schedules. Help me build a single payment calendar so I stop missing them, and tell me my total remaining obligation by week for the next 2 months.

depth_note: Tests BNPL consequence analysis: late fees, credit reporting, and recovery after a missed Klarna payment.
prompt: I missed a $85 Klarna payment by 11 days — $35 late fee, and now they're threatening to report it. I have 3 other Klarna plans in good standing. Will one late payment hit my credit report, does it affect my Klarna spending power, and what's the fastest way to fix the damage?

depth_note: Tests effective-APR exposure on rent-to-own: $3,800 total for a $900 couch.
prompt: A rent-to-own store wants $89 a week for 43 weeks for a couch that retails for $900 — $3,827 total. Show me the effective APR of this deal, what I'd pay if I saved $89 a week for 10 weeks and bought it outright instead, and why these stores target people with bad credit.

depth_note: Tests high-cost auto comparison: rent-to-own car at $400/mo vs buy-here-pay-here loan.
prompt: I need a car and have a 520 credit score. A rent-to-own lot offers a 2018 sedan at $400 a month for 36 months with no ownership until the last payment — $14,400 total for a car worth $9,000. A buy-here-pay-here dealer offers the same car at $350 a month for 36 months at 24% APR. Which is the worse deal in real dollars, and is there a third option I'm missing?
